utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Since no preliminaries were announced, the witness may be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, there was greeting again. This really is the last warning. If you do it again, you'll be removed from the courtroom. Is that clear to you? And this is valid not only for today. We are not going to repeat it every day. You just should following the instructions. No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. Good morning, Mr. Trkulja. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left it off with a document relative to the system of work and drafting reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to calling up 1D02986.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you'll see a document before you. I believe that it is on the screen now. Please look at it and look at the heading where it says: "Main Staff, Army of Republika Srpska." The date is 11 July 1995. In other words, 11 July 1995. We will come back to this page, but I would first like to look at the last page of the same document. In the lower left corner, Colonel, there are initials, NT-PM, would you please explain the Trial Chamber the meaning of these initials?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: NT, that's me. And PM, I can't remember. I believe that those are the initials of the typists who typed the document. Whoever drafted a report or any other document was supposed to place his initials on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you drafted this report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's go back to the first page. On the 11th of July, 1995, who was this document sent to?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only on that date but every day documents were sent to the president of Republika Srpska and corps commanders for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at paragraph 6 on page 3 of both B/C/S and English versions of this document. Paragraph 6. And now in the English version, can we go to the following page because I will draw the witness's attention to the next passage in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here, under (b): "The situation in the corps," and it is the Drina Corps. It says: "... the main forces are being used to mount a persistent defence and part of the forces are involved in offensive operations around ... Srebrenica enclave. In the course of the day, our forces entered the town of Srebrenica. We will forward you an interim report on the results achieved and on other details relating to the offensive operations carried out in the Srebrenica enclave." Further on, there is reference to combat and casualties. My question to you, sir, is this: What was the source of your information when you drafted this report and sent it to the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that was based on the reports of corps commands, one of them being a report by the Drina Corps. I summarised these reports which came on three or four pages. I summarised those reports into one or two paragraphs and I drafted my own report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, were you allowed to include into such a report information that you did not receive from the Drina Corps but from elsewhere, from another source?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First and foremost, we could not obtain any other information from anywhere. Secondly, the only information we had were reports from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were drafting this report, where were you physically?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment - when I say, "at that moment," I mean on that date - we were all in a shelter. However many -- we were at the command post prior to that and after that, that would be done in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say here, and I quote: "We will forward you an interim report on the results achieved and on other details relating to the offensive." What would such an interim report be based on?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Drina Corps submitted an interim report, then we could draft our own interim report. If they didn't do that, then we couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up 1D02987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering the last document we have seen on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will tender both documents because I think they make up a whole and I thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now we have a document in front of us. Again the date is 11 July 1995. It was sent to the Main Staff by the command of the Drina Corps. Its title is: "Interim combat report." Look at bullet point 3: "A decision for the upcoming [sic] operations, consolidate combat disposition along the lines reached and secure the success achieved. After the necessary regrouping, continue the attack with the objective of defeating the enemy completely in the Srebrenica enclave." When it comes to the content of the interim combat report as you see it in front of you, does it reflect the common practice, i.e., that such information about the continuation of engagement would be submitted to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have such cases before so I wouldn't use the word "common practice." I suppose that the president was particularly informed about this, that this information was included into the regular combat report on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember ever having seen or forwarded this information received by the Drina Corps that night between the 11th and 12th of July to the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, mind you, it was 20 years ago, I -- I don't think so. I don't think I did. That's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter 1D02986 and 1D02987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 1D02986 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1043, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And 1D02987 would receive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1043 and D1044 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please tell us whether you remember that night between 11 and 12, which officers were present at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember that. General Miletic was there. I was there. Colonel Sladojevic. And there was a pilot whose name was either Pajic or Pejic. He was there only briefly and that's why his name escapes me. And the encoder whose name was Tihomir. And Gvero used to pop in every now and then around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Around that time, from the 10th until the 20th of July 1995, did you see General Mladic? Did you have any encounters with him at the command of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you just repeat exactly what your question was because in the English version, we get "from the 10th until the," what day of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 20th July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your intervention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please tell us whether you remember that around the time you received a specific order to leave the command post in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question somehow. Since the forces had been broked up -- broken up and they were roaming around, we had to secure the command post at night. I received my task from Miletic on the 16th in the evening, and the task was to go to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When was that in the evening of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was late afternoon, early evening. I can't remember the time. It was either 1700 or 1600 hours. Sladojevic and I received an order to go to the command of the Drina Corps and an officer was supposed to take us to where we wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and let me ask you something really important. To the best of your recollection, what was the exact wording of the order? What was your task?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, it was to inspect the front line to and to raise the security and vigilance of the combatants on the front line in order to prevent or reduce losses. There were a lot of groups that were infiltrating from Srebrenica and those men were simply roaming our -- positions behind our back. That was the essence of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of Colonel Sladojevic as a person who was supposed to share that task with you. What was Colonel Sladojevic's position in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had just joined the Main Staff. He was a member of the operations organ together with Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at P1513. Could we please focus on the first paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is entitled: "Interim combat report." It is sent by the command of the Zvornik Brigade on the 16th of July, 1995, to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please take a look at the very bottom of this document. Could we see who the author of the document is. And then we're going to go back to paragraph 1. In the English version, could we please move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is signed by?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the stamp that is here, it was sent at 1810 on the 16th of July, and then there is this abbreviation RPT at 2005. And then what is handwritten is that due to a bad relay line, the telegram was repeated several times. However, now let us look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so. Witness, and it's at the bottom, it says "Komandant" and then "P potpukovnik." Do you know what the "P" stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-colonel, potpukovnik. Vinko Pandurevic was a lieutenant-colonel then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understood that potpukovnik is a lieutenant-colonel, but there is an another P and then a dot before that. Do you know what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a typo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because it really makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this report, that is to say, on the 16th of July, 1995, Pandurevic says, it says, inter alia, that the units of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army of -- fired almost 1.000 projectiles of varying calibre, parts of the Srebrenica 28th Infantry Battalion together with previously infiltrated groups carried out a synchronised attack against the 4th pb, our positions, weapons, and other equipment from the Planinci and Potocari areas, using their numerical advantage they surrounded the 4th pb. Counting soldiers and civilians, armed and unarmed, together about 7.000. There were examples of attacking and jumping on tanks and self-propelled guns so that by throwing themselves on them, they captured three of our 76-millimetre self-propelled guns. By continuous pressure from the front, they managed to seize three of our trenches in the Poljana area and link up part of their forces with the others in the wider area of Baljkovici. Please let us look at paragraph 3 now. It's in the middle, Colonel. "In order to prevent losses in our own ranks, I have decided in view of the situation to open a corridor along the line of the three lost trenches for the civilian population and there were about 5.000 of them. I have agreed on a method of evacuation with the enemy side and this is now going forward." There is my question: On the 16th of July, 1995, when you received this report to go to the area of the Zvornik Brigade, did you have any information such as those contained in this combat report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be a bit more extensive with regard to this question. This report was never forwarded to the Main Staff by the Drina Corps. That's one thing. When I set out, we had no idea whatsoever about this situation. I did and no one else did at the command post. I first read this report in 2007 when this gentleman gave it to me when I attended the trial. And Pandurevic sent it to his corps and it seems that that's where it ended, because Milos did not have that. I mean, we were there at the command post. This never reached us, none of this. And that's why we had -- I mean, raising alertness and vigilance, I personally was convinced, because I was there -- I mean, it wasn't him. It wasn't he that was there at the command post in that area. It was Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, may I put one question at this moment. You said, Witness, you referred to a certain Milos. What is his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I ask you whom you are referring to when you say "because Milos did not have that." You don't understand that. I read the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Miletic not Milos. Bad translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I read in the transcript: "The first I read this report in 2007 when this gentleman gave it to me when I attended the trial. And Pandurevic sent it to his corps and it seems that that's where it ended, because Milos did not have that." Was that Miletic you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miletic. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just if I may, one point -- another point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At line -- transcript page 10, so 9 to 10, lines 25 and 1, counsel posed the question and referred to "when you received this report to go to the area of the Zvornik Brigade." It's not clear whether counsel's referring to a report or if that's a reference to the order that the witness spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say page 10, line 25, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's page 9, line 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- and it goes on to page 10, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you could clarify this issue with the witness, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that, again, we have this practical misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That evening, did you get a report from General Miletic that evening or an order to go to the area of the Zvornik Brigade on the next day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just an order. I already said that this report never arrived at the command of the Main Staff. I first saw it in 2007, and I can guarantee that Miletic had never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at 1D02989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that -- Could you explain why you can guarantee that Miletic had never seen it? He may have seen it in your absence. He may have seen it one or two days later. Is there -- what makes you so certain that he never saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, all these reports are gathered in one place. And then when I go, I take all the reports at Miletic's so that I could review my map of the armoured units, et cetera. I mean, there was no such report in that place where they're all put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is why you assume or conclude that he has never seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that basis, because when I'm absent I'm not there. Then I have to take all these reports and then I have to take a look at this and to review my own working map. There was no report like this there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. You didn't find it where you would expect it to be if it would have come to his attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, now have you this document before you. It's a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The date is the 16th of July, 1995. And, again, I would like to ask that we move to the last page and then we will go back. In the lower left-hand corner, we see initials again, NT. And my question shall be whether these initials confirm that you wrote this report as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let us go back to the first page for a moment. Who is this report sent to dated the 16th of July? Is this the usual procedure that you have already spoken about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time while I was at the front, this is the procedure that was applied. That is to say, it was sent to the president of the republic and CC'd to the commands of the corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear Mr. Stojanovic's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters did not hear your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at paragraph 6 of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to another page, I have a question with respect to paragraph -- page 1. You said, Mr. Trkulja, that that was sent to the president of the RS and the corps commands. Please look at the last entry. I see there: "VRS GS, IKM-2." What stands that for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forward command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means not only to the commands of the corps but also to the forward command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can move on now? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Another question. If it went to the Main Staff, the forward command post of the Main Staff, does it mean Mr. Mladic would have been aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the forward command post was near Bihac, I cannot it, I mean, define this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "define."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whether -- I mean, where, which forward command post it went to. What forward command posts these are. That is what I cannot ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But were these reports also sent to the Main Staff for the attention of Mr. Mladic; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember whether the Main Staff had a forward command post there or whether that was the forward command post of the Drina Corps, and I know that there was a forward command post near Bihac because that's where Manojlo Milovanovic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document says the forward command post of the Main Staff, but that's not my last question. My last question is: Do these documents that -- the kind of reports that you drafted, did they also be -- got sent to Mr. Mladic for his information or action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These reports were only there for the sake of information about the situation in the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Were they sent to Mr. Mladic also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't define whether that was the theatre of war of the Drina Corps, whether this was the forward command post of the Drina Corps or whether it was the forward command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, again you're not answering my question. I'm not asking you to define that forward command post. I'm asking whether these reports were sent to Mr. Mladic as well. You can either say yes or no, or if you don't know, you say you don't know. But, you know, you were the author of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't know. I'll tell you why I'm asking you these questions because yesterday -- yesterday you were emphatic that these reports never went to Mr. Mladic. You said he never saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that about regular reports. Those that we wrote all the time. This is a very specific individual case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you didn't make that exception yesterday. You said the reports that you drafted he never saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the bulk of them. This is an exception which I didn't remember. I have only remembered it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I leave it at that point. Okay, that's fine. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put a follow-up question. You said a minute ago it is unclear if it was the forward command post of the Main Staff or the Drina Corps. If you read that, it is very clear that it is written "VRS GS, IKM-2." Is it possible that this refers to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say something about the witness who was supposed to come after me. He is versed in these things. A communications guy. He was the one who did that. He is the best suited to explain this because these guys were the ones who established communication and they knew who the communication was between. So you should ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are sitting in front of me as a witness in this trial. You told -- you just told us that this could be the forward command post of the Main Staff or of the Drina Corps. Are you serious about that? It is clearly stated: "VRS GS," which, in my understanding, stands for Main Staff of the VRS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it is written there "IKM-2." What is IKM-2 of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes, yes. It's a forward command post, but I've told you that there was another forward command post near Bihac as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, you said that, near Bihac. And that might be the reason why we see here the number 2. Which one is it? I'm asking you as a member of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's number 2 forward command post, because number 2 man was there, Manojlo, near Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I then ask you where forward command post 1 was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. Whatever I were to say now would be mere speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say the other one was in Bihac but you don't know where the first one was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know the sector. I know that it wasn't in Bihac, but where exactly it was near Bihac, I don't know. It was in the western theatre of war. I don't know its exact position. It was a long time ago, 20 years. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where, then, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had anything to say, I would, but I'm not sure about anything. Nothing's certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what comes to your mind even though it's not certain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the command activities took place at the forward command post of the Drina Corps. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm talking about forward command post number 2 of the VRS Main Staff. And as a matter of fact, I'm asking -- we started with number 2 and I now asked where number 1 was, VRS Main Staff forward command post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since none of the chiefs of army branches was engaged at forward command post 1, so I don't think it existed. I suppose that all the command activities took place at the command post of the Drina Corps. Nobody was engaged at the forward command post 1. There were people at the forward command post 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that no one was at the forward command post number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that my colleagues went with Manojlo and only four of us were -- stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stayed where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the command post in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the command post, not a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it was the command post. And when it comes to forward command post 1, I don't think so. Nobody was engaged there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did it exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my doubts about that. Since -- serious doubts. Because none of the Command Staff were -- was engaged there. I suppose everything went through the forward command post of the Drina Corps. All the activities took place there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We left it off with the document on the screen. I'd like to look at paragraph 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this report, which was sent to the addressees that you had an opportunity to see a while ago, under 6 (a) it says that the enemy in front of the 1st zvbk regrouped large forces and used them early in the morning in a strong artillery and infantry attack on our unit's sector along the Baljkovicka Reka-Pandurica axis. They were co-ordinating with the forces pulling out from the former Srebrenica enclave. They were able to breakthrough the defence and capture three trenches notice Baljkovici village sector, create a corridor and so on and so forth. Colonel, when it comes to this type of information about the situation in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, would it be considered dramatic, would it call for a need to look at the situation on the front line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's a leading question. He can be asked about more generally the same thing without suggesting to him whether it's dramatic or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also asks for opinion. Could you please rephrase your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in military terms, you, as an officer of the Main Staff, would such information imply a need for additional information as to what was going on in the zone of one of your brigades?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is dramatic. I went there. We'll come to that later. However, the report portrays the situation even more dramatic than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second phrasing of your question was as leading as the first one. Would you try to understand what proper court practice means. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when did you embark on the mission that you had received from Miletic the previous evening?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th, in the morning hours. Sladojevic and I -- myself got into a Puch, there was a driver who drove it, and we went to Vlasenica and we stopped in front of the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll stop you here for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to tender 1D02989 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1045, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived in front of the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We pulled over and a colonel asked us what was going on. They already knew that they were supposed to give us an officer who would accompany us to the Zvornik Brigade and to the front line. A major - whose family name I can't remember - joined us and went with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please describe the further course of your activities and your movement towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on our way to Zvornik, and when we got close to the Konjevic Polje cross-road, Sladojevic said: There's so much talk about Srebrenica, why don't we go and see what is going on there. And instead of proceeding towards Zvornik we diverted towards Bratunac and we entered Srebrenica. And there's not much there, just one street. We drove along that street to its end, we turned around, the driver turned around, and then we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about your perception of Srebrenica at the moment when you passed through -- through it.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were passing through Srebrenica, we drove slowly and there were people there, they returned to their houses. They were cleaning their front yards. Nothing special was going on. There were throwing out garbage from their houses. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stop in Srebrenica anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never even got out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Zvornik, to the command post of the Zvornik Brigade. A captain was there waiting for us. I don't know whether he was an active-duty officer or reserve officer. The major exchanged a few words with him. I told him that I wanted to go to Crni Vrh and I didn't know the way. We needed somebody to take us there. They appointed somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you entered the building of the Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were standing in front of the building, and we dealt with all the issues there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who took you to the Crni Vrh sector from the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. I didn't know the way, and that's why we were accompanied to Vlasenica and to the brigade command by some people who were familiar with the area. They took us where Sladojevic and I had planned to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when was it on the 17th of July, 1995, when you arrived in the Crni Vrh sector?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was late in the afternoon, or early evening. Major Obrenovic turned up. He reported to me. That's why I am saying that the reports that were previously sent, on the previous day, things were overly dramatised because the situation was not nearly as dramatic as described in the reports. Because they were in a ditch. They had not managed to break through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazic appeared from the Drina Corps, and Obrenovic reported to him as well. And night fell and he took us to a monastery where we were supposed to spend the night. I don't know the name of the monastery but it wasn't that far from Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, in a report that you received from Obrenovic, were there any references to the casualties on both sides?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he did not have any specific information. He knew that the self-propelling guns crews were injured but he couldn't tell me any numbers. That's why I am telling you that this report overly dramatises the situation on -- on the ground. The front line had not been broken through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how far is the monastery from the place where you spoke to Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - and mind you, I don't know the area - I believe that it was about 4 kilometres away. It is very difficult to assess because the road was not very good and the vehicle could not travel fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I believe that this is the time for our first break. We will continue. In any case, I'm going to put another question to you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is the time for a break and then I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need after the break, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have another document. I believe that I will need about 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes, that's okay. Witness, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, it was announced that there was a preliminary from the Prosecution, Defence, a translation to be uploaded? To be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can deal can it now or at the beginning of my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do it -- if it is just announcing which new translation should replace which one, then we can deal with it in half a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've received a final revised translation for P1655. This was admitted through RM316 on the 2nd of July, 2013, transcript page 13661. The revised translation is uploaded under doc ID 0086-9331-1 ET. And we'd request that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll do that perhaps later today. Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, if you remember, we stopped at the moment when you said that you spent the night between the 17th and 18th in that monastery. I'm just asking you whether you remember who it was that spent the night there at that monastery?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about Lazic. I, Sladojevic, Vasic, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear who else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been quite a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat. You mentioned Lazic. You, yourself, Sladojevic, Vasic -- and did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say Vasic. The major from the Vlasenica Corps -- no, the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, where did you go from the monastery?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had breakfast there and we returned to the same place from where we had left the previous evening when we went to the monastery, so it was that place by Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on that morning, who did you have contact with as for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that Pandurevic was -- actually, Lazic went on with us and there were some other officers. I didn't know most of them. I'm mentioning the ones that I did know. I, Sladojevic, the major, then Lazic. Pandurevic, I saw him there, and there were others. As far as I remember, it was a large group, quite large.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who informed you then about the situation -- about the situation in the defence area of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, no one. The previous day, Obrenovic informed us about everything. We were there -- and I didn't bring my spectacles that day. That was a mistake. The younger ones could see better. That was an omission on my part. The column was passing, the one that was at the ditch. That was that only activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if the witness says that Mr. Obrenovic informed about everything, then it may not be easy for the Chamber to understand exactly what this information was. Could even be misunderstood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to tell us, to the best of your recollection, what kind of information you received that afternoon from Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrenovic informed us that there had been fighting there in front of Crni Vrh and that he happened to be nearby. He had three tanks. He's a tank man anyway. And he managed to push back the enemy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So everything happened, happened only through combat activities. And then he explained to me that through the Motorola - there weren't mobile phones then - he established contact with the leader of that group and that they agreed that they would open the front and that they would let them go. And that's why I said that this was a report that was sent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear part of it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report was dramatised. The situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, two times the interpreters now had to tell us that you didn't -- that they were unable to hear everything you said. So would you both slow down and speak up. Mr. Stojanovic, it's your witness. You're best in a position to see what still needs to be clarified or what is not of such relevance that you would revisit it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm following the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, for the transcript, for the record, you said at one moment that from that report, you had the opportunity to receive information about communication with the enemy side regarding the possibility of opening this corridor. I'm just asking you to tell us, for the record, how this communication took place? Through what kind of communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago Motorola. That's how contact was established. Obrenovic and the leader of that group that was in the ditch, and they agreed that they would open it, that they would de-mine, that they would allow two platoons, and then they would pass there. It was only the 17th when he said that to me. They de-mined that. They withdrew the platoons, and it was only the next day, around 10.00, that the pullout started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, on that occasion, did you have any information concerning the possible existence of POWs?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no POWs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot understand what the witness is saying. Could he please slow down. Could all other microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you resume from when -- could you resume from where you said: "There were no POWs ..." Could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Stojanovic is again invited to switch off his microphone while the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no POWs. This was happening at one moment, combat, tanks, they withdrew. They stopped and communication started when there was a separation between the forces. That's the explanation that Obrenovic gave me. And they agreed that they would let them go. These two platoons would leave the position and it was agreed that the pullout would happen the next day. And I was present with those officers that I mentioned a moment ago, and that's when they were pulling out, the following day. It started the next day at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you return from the sector of Crni Vrh to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say approximately now that it was more than two hours. It lasted for two hours. Even longer than that. I cannot be precise now. I cannot say, 12, 13, I know that it was during the day, that it was past midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon returning to Crna Rijeka, when you returned to the Main Staff who did you find there, as far as officers are concerned?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one at the command post in Crna Rijeka was General Miletic, no one else. I told him about the entire situation, what happened, how it happened, and how it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever take a written report about going to the area of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not submit a report and no one asked me for a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for your information and observations in the area of the Zvornik Brigade, did you ever report to General Mladic about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I couldn't have because I did not have any communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at document 65 ter 04028.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are we are waiting for that, Mr. Stojanovic, one question for the witness. You're telling us what Obrenovic said on the morning of the 18th of July, 1995. No word was said about persons that were detained or had been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, Obrenovic spoke to me on the 17th in the evening. On the 18th, I already knew. There was not a single word about POWs, detainees, there were no such people. We were out in the open, all of us. There was no one there. No camp, no nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you hadn't heard anything about larger numbers of people being detained and people that would have died --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- after having been captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, Your Honour, the only people who were suppressed in combat were in the ditch and it was agreed that they would be released once the front line was open. Nothing else. There was nothing else on either of the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not on what had happened on the days before? I mean, I can imagine that if you have a small number of people that you -- which are still alive, that you take some action. But not a word about what had happened the days before? In terms of detention and possibly persons having died even after having been captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue using this document, just one question: Colonel, did Colonel Lazic return together with you? What happened to Colonel Lazic, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I really can't define -- no, he was not with us in the vehicle. I don't know whether he got into any other vehicle and when. There were the three of us in the vehicle. We left the major behind and we proceeded in our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now please look at the document in front of you. It is a document by the Main Staff of the VRS issued on the 17th of July, 1995. Its title is: "Integration operations to crush lagging Muslim forces." It is an order. At the bottom, you can see that it was authored by Commander Colonel General Ratko Mladic. Under 1 it says: "Send three officers (Colonels Nedeljko Trkulja, Milovan Stankovic, and Bogdan Sladojevic) from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to the command of the 1st zpbr to assist in the joining of the VRS and MUP forces, the planning and co-ordination of combat operations to block, crush, and destroy lagging Muslim forces in the wider areas of Kamenica and Cerska." Under 2 it says: "The team from the VRS GS shall assess the situation on the brigade's front line and in the rear, the available forces, and hear out the proposal and opinion of the commander of the 1st zpbr. On this basis, they are to draw up a plan together with the brigade commander to comb the terrain, to block, crush, and destroy the struggling parts of armed Muslim groups in the general area of Kamenica, Cerska, and Udrc." My question: Colonel Trkulja, did you have this order by General Mladic in your hands at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, this order, when it was drafted, I was already on my field mission. Secondly, this order was never implemented. When I returned, I reported verbally to Miletic. Therefore, all the problems that are listed here had already been resolved, and this was not necessary at all. There was no need for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me finish with the following question: Colonel, sir, during those war years, did you have any opportunity to participate in preparations and making proposals for decisions and orders that Ratko Mladic was supposed to issue as the commander of the VRS Main Staff? Do you know anything about that process? Were you ever a part of that process?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, thank you for these answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter 04028 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1046, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Before we continue, I briefly would like to instruct Mr. Registrar to replace the current translation for P1655 by the newly uploaded one known under doc ID number 0086-9331-1 ET. And if there's any problem with the newly uploaded translation, the Defence may revisit the matter within the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a question with respect to the document which is still on our screen, D1046. Mr. Trkulja, we see here an order. To whom was this order issued? I see at the top: "To the Drina Corps Command, for information." But who was the real addressee of the order who had to carry out the details of this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was to be received by General Miletic. I suppose he did receive it. I was already on my field mission. And when I returned, as I've already told you, whatever is mentioned in here had already been resolved. So that order never actually was implemented. There was no need for it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. I would like to know where can I find the addressee of this order? Who should carry out the task issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was supposed to do it. But this was never given to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was not sent to you. I see there 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- 1st Bratunac Brigade, Milici Brigade, and the 67th Communications Regiment. Are these the addressees of the order to carry out the task listed here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, I read: "Send three officers," including you, "from the Main Staff of the VRS to the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade to assist in the joining of the VRS and MUP," and so on. Who should send you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Miletic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Miletic. There was nobody else. He was the most senior officer at the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it -- is this -- please have a look on this document. Was that addressed to the command post of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were not at the forward command post. We were at our permanent command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see you're not able to identify who is the real addressee of this order to send you to the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade. Another question. You several times said everything had been resolved at that time. What do you mean by that? What was resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main forces that were in the rear of the Zvornik Brigade crossed the front line and went in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean the main forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And how do I have to understand in paragraph 1 of this document "the joining of the VRS and MUP forces"? What was that about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just bear with me, please. This was written because they didn't know that I was already on a field mission, that things had already been agreed and resolved, that the burning issue had already been dealt with. This would have been done and implemented if those forces had remained behind the lines of the Zvornik Brigade. Since they left, a new group was never set up. None of the things mentioned in the order were ever implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that, that there was no co-operation or resubordination of the VRS and the MUP forces? What is the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was supposed to be the one to regulate that. Since the matter was resolved, I never went to the Zvornik Brigade again at that time because there was no need for that. That order was never implemented. It never took off the ground, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How -- what is the source of your knowledge that such a co-operation whatsoever was never carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about that short period of time I was supposed to participate in that together with Sladojevic and the late Stankovic. We didn't. There was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few follow-up questions as well. And for the first question, I'm also asking the special attention of the parties because there may be an ambiguity in the text of this document. When my colleague, Judge Fluegge, read a second ago to whom the order was addressed, he read: "To the Drina Corps, for information." I asked myself whether it is to the Drina Corps for information and then a few other brigades are mentioned, or whether it is to the Drina Corps, for information, then the following brigades that are mentioned, and I'm specifically paying attention to the comma after the abbreviation for Drina Corps, DK. Witness, having listened to this and having looked at the document, do you consider it a possibility that the Drina Corps was the addressee of this very urgent order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They received it just for information purposes because they had to know who was supposed to carry that out, I was supposed to be the one, and that they wouldn't be engaged because the team consisting of Sladojevic and myself, we would be in charge of that and those units were to report to me. Everything had been resolved and that order was never implemented. It never took off the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I understand you well, the Main Staff of the VRS is issuing an order to that same Main Staff, or to you, that you should send yourself to do something. Is that how I have to understand this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Not me personally. It was sent to Miletic. And Miletic, in his turn, was supposed to give me that task, tell me what to do, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now where do you find, then, again, where do you finds that Miletic is the one who should execute this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miletic was the most senior officer at the command post. Whatever was received, he was supposed to receive it, and he was supposed to convey orders to the rest of us who were there. He was the one who was supposed to tell us what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have another question. You said everything had been dealt with, had been resolved already. Now I see in paragraph 5 of this order, I see that the terrain still had to be cleared up. Was that done already immediately? That takes a while, isn't it, because you needed the competent municipal organ, manpower should be provided from the civilian protection to clear up the terrain. Was that all done already? Was there no need to do that any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when this was drafted, the situation was unknown. On the 17th, most of the forces left. After that, nobody had to be engaged. Not the civilian protection, not the police. I was not required to form a group consisting of those units because the main issue had been resolved. The forces that were behind the lines of the Zvornik Brigade had crossed over to the other side, and that was it. That was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber received evidence that in the departure or in the moving out of members of the armed forces of BiH, that a lot may have died when moving out and were still in the terrain. Were you -- was that something you knew or do you say that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the operation of pullout on the 18th, not a single bullet was fired from any piece of weapon on either side. There were casualties, there were dead, but at the time, that was not known. Those people had been killed during combat one or two days before. Only later would the information become known. I'm talking about the 17 and the 18. On the 18, not a single bullet was fired, nobody was captured. The -- two militaries were separated. On the one hand there were the 5.000 soldiers and on the other side there was the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm asking you this because in the order it -- apparently there seems to be a need to clear up the terrain. You said everything had been resolved, although I didn't hear anything about the clearing up of the terrain already being done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've told you, the order came too late because the bulk of the issues facing the Zvornik Brigade had been resolved. After that, there was no need to set up a unit because most of the Muslim soldiers had already crossed over. That order was simply belated. It became moot. It was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're emphasising that those who were still alive had moved out and there was no need to do anything with them. My question is about those who were -- who stayed behind and were not alive anymore, whether there was any need to clear up the terrain as this order says has to be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't participate in that. When the column left, we left as well. I don't know whether the Zvornik Brigade picked up the dead, whether they cleared the terrain or not. I don't know. I don't know anything about that because I did not participate in any of those activities, and none of that ever reached us in any of the reports, so I really was not in a position to know what they did after we left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier you said there was no need for anything to be -- still to be done, and now you're telling me that you did not participate in such activities of which you do not know whether it still had to be done. But I'll leave it to that. You'll now be further cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You find Ms. Hasan to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. Carefully listen to her questions and answer them in a decent speed of speech and loudly, clearly speaking. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, I will be using an intercept which we have a revised translation for. It's P1330, admitted on the 2nd of May, 2013. There is one word in the intercept that has been changed. And the revised translation has been uploaded under doc ID 0321-5958-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you want me to instruct Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to replace the current translation by the newly uploaded one. Could you tell us what triggered the change? And is the Defence aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We sent an e-mail to the Defence yesterday, the 4th of May. And what triggered the need for it is I had reviewed the intercept and the wording of it didn't seem right, and I requested that they review it. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, no problems with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, you're hereby instructed to replace the current English translation of P1330 by the newly uploaded one, uploaded under doc ID 0321-5958-ET. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified about the reporting procedure to the Supreme Commander Dr. Karadzic and you were asked about that and you were asked questions by Judge Orie and today you were also asked about that, about General Mladic's knowledge of such reports, of the content of those reports that went to the Supreme Commander. And this can be found at transcript pages 35074 and 35075 of yesterday's transcript. And you responded yesterday that he was not informed but that he could have gone downstairs at the command post the next day to look at such reports if he had wanted to. And today, in looking at the 16 July report to the Supreme Commander, you mentioned that that may have been an exception, a report that did -- what -- that was brought to General Mladic's attention. Now, Judge Orie asked a similar question to General Milovanovic in this case. And this is at transcript page 16963, starting at line 14. I'm going to read you the question and General Milovanovic's response. So Judge Orie asks: "Now, even if General Mladic did not sign that report to the Supreme Command on every day, would he still be aware of the content of what was reported to the Supreme Command?" General Milovanovic says: "Yes. As I've already told you once, whenever there were any changes or wherever there were developments in the military, I would report to him on the -- and them as soon as I met him. Those reports that I sent to the Supreme Command would end up on his desk as well as the reports by the subordinate commands, if it was my assessment that he should be put in the picture. I didn't send him all of the reports because he would have ended up with piles of paper. I made a selection, and I only sent him those things that I thought he should be made aware of." If you bear with me, he goes on at transcript page 16964, starting at line 7, and he says: "For example, if General Mladic was not in the Main Staff, if he was not in his command post, the staff would continue to function as if he had been there. However, I could not wait for General Mladic to return for him to look at the report to sign it, and to send it to the Supreme Command. It had to be there by midnight. If General Mladic turned up in the morning during the regular meeting, he and the entire staff would be informed about the reports that had arrived from the units and what the Supreme Command received as our report." You don't dispute what General Milovanovic has testified to, do you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. Contesting just one part. And I stand by what I said yesterday. You can check and see that Ratko Mladic did not sign a single report. Milovanovic did not take any of them to him. They were encoded and then carried to him by couriers who were dispatched by me. When the report was encoded that piece of paper returned to me. If what Milovanovic is saying is true, then you would have Ratko Mladic's signatures everywhere, and still there are none.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let me be clear because I didn't read to you what General Milovanovic had testified just before being asked that question. He had said that such reports were not signed by General Mladic because it would have been too much of a burden to have him sign that every day at that late time of day, and so it would be his responsibility to sign those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask for clarification in the meantime. Sir, at page 41, lines 11, you say: "Milovanovic did not take any of them to him. They were encoded and then carried to him by couriers who were dispatched by me." What do you -- who is the "him" you are referring to whom encoded reports were taken by courier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would write a report. I would send it to Milovanovic so that he would sign it. Once he signs it, then the courier would arrive and he would take it to the encoder, the communications man who would encode it and send to the president of the republic and CC it to the corps. That's what happened every day. Now what Milovanovic said, it is possible that it's only correct when there is some extreme, extraordinary thing taking place. The rest is not correct. What is correct is what I'm saying and that can be checked. You can see that Mladic didn't sign that anywhere and that did not reach him at all. If he is interested, he would go down to the ops centre, he can read whichever report he wants to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, and it may have been that I didn't give you the context of what Milovanovic had said, but let's be clear, Milovanovic did not say that Mladic was signing these reports. What he was saying is that he signed these reports which went to the Supreme Commander but that he left a copy of these reports and any other underlying reports from the corps as he saw necessary to General -- on General Mladic's desk. That's what General Milovanovic is saying. Do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do dispute that because I dictate it so that it's typed up. It is typed in one copy. So then if it's just one copy, there cannot one that is left and another one that is taken away. It is from that copy that the encoder sends that on, encoding it, and also there's a confirmation of that on the back. There were never two copies. So the reports did not arrive to Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Trkulja, let's move on. Now you had been asked yesterday about the Krivaja 95 operation. And this is at transcript page 35072 and 35073, where you said that you didn't personally participate in it and you were not acquainted with the Krivaja 95 operation. You did not have any information about it. You didn't even know its name. Let's leave aside the name of the operation, Krivaja 95. Were you aware of plans in 1995 to attack the Srebrenica enclave and take it over?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at D00298.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I just want to correct my -- my question. I don't know if I had misspoken or if it's transcribed differently but what I meant to say is where you -- were you aware of plans in 1995 to attack the Srebrenica enclave and to eventually take it over? Is your answer still no?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, your reference to the transcript pages of yesterday disappeared, if I see it well, from the today's transcript. Could you please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Transcript pages 35072 to 35073. And Your Honour I can direct you, if you're looking at that, it's lines -- on 35072 lines 18 to 19 and on the next page, lines 20 to 22. Thereabouts are his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, this is a 15 May 1995 urgent order from the deputy commander at the time, Colonel Radislav Krstic, to the commands of various units. And we can flip to the very last pages of this document so you can see that. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What this is, it's an order, as it says in the heading, to stabilize defence around Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and establish conditions for the liberation of the enclaves. In other words, these are Krstic's order to create the necessary conditions for attacking Srebrenica and Zepa. Now, you were at the Main Staff command during this time-period, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you understood that there -- that this was a preliminary order to create a platform for military operations to actually take the Srebrenica enclave? I mean, you were familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That can be seen here. It would have been in the report of the 15th had I been familiar with it. This is just some preparation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So let's move on to next day, 16 May 1995, and look at P2098. What this is, is a regular combat report that goes from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff where you were at. And, again, this is from Krstic, and let's focus on item 2. You'll see here it says: "All Drina Corps units are in full combat readiness and successfully holding the lines reached. We are continuing with the preparations for stabilisation of defence around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in accordance with your order. We are currently unable to implement your order to fully close off the enclaves and carry out the [sic] attacks against them because we do not have sufficient forces, but we are continuing to take specific measures to uncover enemy groups in the gap, detect their combat support and ... of the forward line of defence." Now clearly Krstic here is referring to his ability to implement Main Staff orders; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And he goes on in the next paragraph to report that the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade searched the terrain along the Lisina-Glogic axis and it was observed that a strong enemy group was staying in this sector. And I'm going to get back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: For now, if we can turn to page 2 in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so. Witness, at the heading of this document, I see that IKM-1 of the GS VRS is mentioned. You earlier told us that you thought that the forward command post 1 didn't exist at the time. Any comment on the reference to IKM-1 GS VRS here, which is apparently -- or at least the word "Zvornik" is added? You're still convinced that it didn't exist at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe that's what's written, but, yes, when I went to Zvornik, there was no one there except for a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And why would you think that the Drina Corps command would send a document to the first forward command post of the Main Staff of the VRS if it didn't exist? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why it was sent to Zvornik, I have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there personally on the 17th. There was no one there at that command except for one duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it's our understanding that this forward command post related to the Spreca operation what was going on at that time in May 1995 and that there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a month --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- a possible difference in July that the forward command post was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that there's a month of time difference here, and I do understand that the Prosecution interprets in its own way, that it's not necessarily at the same location. You could put that to the witness if you want to, but I leave that to you, whether you want to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, you were aware of the Spreca operation, weren't you? This is the operation --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you just very briefly, in just a couple of sentences, tell us what that involved.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was some attack. I cannot remember exactly, the exact location. I know that I sent a tank company from the protection regiment to that area. It's been a very long time.
